newsitem.title: USA: Fannie, Freddie respond to Congress on loan limit.
newsitem.headline: Fannie, Freddie respond to Congress on loan limit.

text.p: The Federal National Mortgage Association and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp, responding to Congressional pressure, said Thursday they would take into account past home price index declines when setting next year's loan limit.
The two firms set their loan limits each year based on the Federal Housing Finance Board's October home price survey and its change from the previous October.
The loan limit establishes a ceiling for loans that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase. Currently that ceiling is $207,000.
A Congressional aide said indications from this year's home price survey show that Fannie and Freddie could raise the 1997 loan limit to about $227,000 if past decreases are not taken into account.

Legislation introduced in the House would have required past losses in the home price index to be taken into account before the loan limit could be increased. The bill was not taken up before Congress adjourned, and its sponsors said they planned to proceed with it next year.
Under that legislation, the loan limit for 1997 would be about $217,000, the Congressional aide said.

Three House Banking Committee members -- Rep. Rick Lazio, R-NY, Rep. Richard Baker, R-La., and Paul Kanjorski, D-Pa. -- last week sent a letter to the chairmen of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac seeking voluntary compliance with the intent of the proposed legislation.

"The objection is their charter is to serve low- and moderate-income people, and (with) this thing going unchecked they'd end up capturing the entire market, we've got other financial players out there that serve the upper end," the Congressional aide said.
"We will be pleased to comply with the provisions of this legislation in setting the 1997 mortgage ceiling," Fannie Mae Chairman James Johnson wrote in a letter to Lazio.

Leland Brendsel, chairman of Freddie Mac, wrote that the firm would net out past decreases when raising the loan limit, but "as a matter of public policy, I continue to believe that as many families as possible should have access to the tremendous benefits of the secondary market..."
